articles.title: Wall Street's big CoreWeave stock bear is now even more bearish
articles.summary: CoreWeave continues to be a hotly debated stock.
articles.body:
So much for a bullish tone from Elon Musk on AI demand during his SpaceX ( SPCX ) earnings call, arresting the slide in CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and other neocloud stocks.

At least as seen through the eyes of one of Wall Street's biggest CoreWeave bears.

Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei slashed her price target on the stock to $51 from $74 on Thursday and maintained an Underperform rating.

"We caught a lot of hate when we initiated on CRWV with a $56 price target seven months ago. Today, it's a lot harder to find bulls—certainly some of them just don't call us anymore, but there seems to be more broad acceptance of the challenges of this business model. Could this turn around? Maybe: it's a wildly volatile, momentum-driven stock, but barring major moves, the fundamentals are probably stuck," Rezaei said.

If there is any positive for the CRWV bulls, Rezaei doesn't think the stock is headed to $0.

"We do not believe CRWV is a 0—they still have a large backlog, line of sight to powered shell delivery, and while we don't think the contracts are super attractive, they're not underwater. Whether Nvidia ( NVDA ) will step in is meatier; we think they would intervene in a true downside. Doesn't necessarily re-energize the stock, but raises the floor," she added.

CoreWeave's stock has been torched in October to the tune of 28%. Shares lost 6% in pre-market trading today.

The company's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet. That has triggered a subsequent sharp sell-off in the stock.

The rise in yields on CoreWeave's bonds even spurred Elon Musk to post "Yikes" on X in response to a post by venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya last week.

Meanwhile, in a new report, Gartner forecast that by 2030, "cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model will force over 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations."

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show and the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast, and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title: Copper Declines as Tech-Stock Selloff Dulls Appetite for Risk
articles.summary: Copper fell with other industrial metals, as a selloff in AI-related stocks sapped risk appetite across global markets.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Copper ( HG=F ) fell with other industrial metals, as a selloff in AI-related stocks sapped risk appetite across global markets.

The red metal slipped as much as 0.7% to $14,260 a ton on the London Metal Exchange. Asian shares slid after earnings from major tech companies failed to reassure investors about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade. Copper has benefited from that boom because of its use in data centers and power infrastructure.

Its retreat from last month's record high of $14,875 a ton has also been fueled by doubts over whether the US will impose a tariff on refined copper as President Donald Trump approaches the midpoint of his second term. The prospect of a levy has drawn vast amounts of the metal into US warehouses this year, squeezing supplies elsewhere.

"There is still a great deal of uncertainty around next year's copper supply-demand balance," said Zhenting Zhou, a trader at Hangzhou Chenglian Industrial Co. "Mine supply should improve, US import demand is likely to ease, and China's scrap-copper availability should also recover. There isn't much upside risk for copper," he said.

Still, some concerns remain around supply disruptions. Workers at Canada's largest copper mine, Teck Resources Ltd.'s Highland Valley Copper operation, are threatening to strike as early as Saturday, in the latest sign of labor tensions prompted by near-record prices that have emboldened employees to seek a greater share of profits.

Copper was 0.4% lower at $14,294.50 a ton on the LME as of 11 a.m. in Shanghai. Aluminum declined 0.6% to $3,023.50, while nickel gave up 1% after surging 3.7% in the prior session on the prospect of coordinated output cuts by Chinese producers in Indonesia.

Iron ore fell as much as 1.7% to $89.45 a ton in Singapore, the lowest in almost two years, before paring losses.

articles.title: The Live Nation Empire That Music Fans Hate is at Risk of a Break Up
articles.summary: Critics say the music giant at the center of an antitrust lawsuit is crowding out independent venues — and making it harder for new acts to break through.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The Crowbar nightclub of Tampa, Florida never looked like much outside: a squat building with painted-over windows in a neighborhood where feral chickens roam brick streets.

Inside was where the magic happened. For 20 years, Crowbar's single, 300-person room served as a place to hear unknown artists before they broke or popular acts offering more intimate shows. Musicians as different as rock band OK Go, country's Kenny Chesney and indie-pop singer Chappell Roan graced its stage. A generation of local rappers honed their skills there.

On July 31, Crowbar closed its doors for the last time, beset by rising costs and the elephant in any discussion about concerts in the US: Live Nation Entertainment Inc. The colossus — which owns arenas and clubs, runs the nation's biggest ticketing service and manages musicians' careers — plans to build its own venue nearby. For Crowbar's final show, rapper Talib Kweli flew down from New York City, with local hip hop artists joining him onstage.

Across the country, some 480 independent venues and 240 music festivals have shut since 2020, with 160 shuttering so far this year, according to the National Independent Venue Association, a trade group for the industry. While the Covid-19 pandemic and surging inflation each played a role, so has the market power of Live Nation, according to Crowbar owner Tom DeGeorge and other independents. They struggle to compete against a $40 billion company that can steer artists to play one venue and avoid others while exerting significant control over ticket pricing through its Ticketmaster subsidiary.

This year, the Trump administration agreed to settle a monopoly case against Live Nation weeks after the company's CEO met with the president. The company denies any political interference. Displeased with the deal, a group of states fought on and, in April, won a landmark jury verdict that the company illegally monopolized live events. Now, those states want a federal judge to take the rare step of ordering a corporate breakup. Independent club owners and many musicians argue it's the only way to bring balance back to the market.

"If Live Nation wasn't the monopoly they were, I think all of our independent venues would have the ability to thrive much more," DeGeorge said in an interview. "When you have one entity that comes in that controls the entire ocean, nobody else gets to swim."

Around 60% of the reductions are expected to affect support functions, including developers, while operational and functional roles will account for most of the job losses.The move comes as Barclays approaches the end of a three-year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking business. Its investment banking division is also affected.In its third-quarter earnings presentation on Thursday, the bank said it was “structurally reducing the cost base to generate capacity for investment.” It described the expected outcome as “organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI.”Barclays said AI was the "icing on the cake" of its wider modernisation strategy. Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts reflected significant investment in technology to simplify and improve the business.Barclays reported pre-tax profit of £2.3 billion ($3.1 billion) for the three months to September, up 12% from the same period a year earlier. Return on tangible equity fell to 11.7% from 16.1%.Barclays shares were almost 1% lower less than an hour into the trading session. Economists are examining company results for evidence that spending on new technology, particularly AI, is improving day-to-day operations, boosting efficiency and reducing staffing requirements.Barclays' latest workforce reduction comes amid this wider scrutiny of how companies are using AI and whether the technology is delivering operational gains.You use AI every day. articles.title: Netflix is losing viewers — but they're still subscribed
articles.summary: People aren't leaving the service, but they aren't watching it enthusiastically, either.
articles.body:
Netflix ( NFLX ) has a unique problem: subscription zombies.

The company is seeing sagging engagement in the US , while also claiming an industry-low churn rate. People aren't leaving the service, but they aren't watching it enthusiastically, either.

If the company's stock price — down 30% this year — is any indication , investors are fed up. But the steep fall from prior highs is, given the right insights and conviction, another buying opportunity.

That's how analysts at Deutsche Bank see things. In a note published Wednesday, Bryan Kraft made the case for buying the dip.

After the company reported third quarter earnings, Netflix shares fell to their lowest level in more than two years as the streaming giant missed estimates on the current quarter's revenue outlook and the full-year ad revenue forecast.

As management acknowledged there's room for its US business to do better , Kraft took a contrarian take.

Netflix viewing continues to grow outside the US, and in every region churn is down compared to last year, in every region, despite recent price hikes, he said.

"We found management's commentary on churn, international viewing, new content leadership, and their long-term growth outlook all pretty encouraging," he said.

The market has fixated on sagging time spent watching and a lackluster slate of content. But Kraft believes this stems from a weaker lineup compared to last year, rather than a deeper decline in quality.

Netflix's stock market struggle and its engagement problem both arrive with a dose of irony. After all, Paramount's ( SKYD ) stated justification for pursuing Warner Bros. was to get big enough to compete with Netflix. But Netflix is looking less like an indomitable tech giant and more like a beleaguered studio struggling to convince American audiences that it isn't a slop factory.

Netflix has a reputation for being the comfort streamer — the limitless provider of pleasant background noise while you fold laundry or try to fall asleep. That has value, of course. But YouTube gives you that for free. And TikTok and Instagram's Reels spare you the mental load of having to choose what to put on.

The recent executive shakeups also suggest that Netflix had ceded, or perhaps never really went after, the sought-after TV shows and movies that people associate with Apple TV and HBO Max.

But Kraft said that the growth outlook for Netflix remains healthy, even with some deceleration next year. There's member growth, price increases, more box office revenue, and advertising to support a more bullish thesis.

articles.title: Tesla is spending less now, but the bill is coming later: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Tesla cut $5 billion from this year's spending plan. It also told investors the bill is going up from here.
articles.body:
Tesla cut $5 billion from this year's spending plan. It also told investors the bill is going up from here.

On Wednesday, Tesla ( TSLA ) lowered its 2026 capital spending guidance to about $20 billion from $25 billion. The cut came after a quarter in which it spent $4.73 billion, about $3.2 billion less than analysts expected, according to Bloomberg estimates. The lighter spending helped Tesla generate $1.53 billion in free cash flow , when Wall Street had braced for it to burn nearly $5 billion.

"Our capex for the next few years would continue to expand as we add more robotaxi fleet, we expand our production capacity for Optimus, install manufacturing capacity for solar, purchase additional SI compute infrastructure, and build a semiconductor fab," Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said on the company's earnings call.

Tesla also lined up the ability to borrow up to $30 billion to support that growth, though Taneja said it doesn't plan to tap the money this year. Shares fell 2% after hours following a 3.4% gain in the regular session.

Through three quarters, Tesla has spent about $13 billion. The new plan leaves roughly $7 billion for the fourth quarter.

That would still be a record, about 20% above the $5.8 billion Tesla spent in the second quarter. But it's well short of what the old plan required: nearly $12 billion in one quarter, more than the $8.5 billion Tesla spent in all of 2025.

The biggest project is just getting started. Musk said Terafab, the chip plant Tesla is building with SpaceX, will need tens of billions of dollars in equipment through early 2028 and likely more than $100 billion over the long term. The two companies still have to work out who pays for what. Real production isn't expected until late 2028.

Spending on other projects is already ramping. Tesla expects to have 400 megawatts of AI training compute running by year-end. It has started Optimus robot production in Fremont, Calif., and is building a second, larger robot factory in Austin.

"We're definitely, as I say in Vegas, betting on the come," Musk said.

articles.title: Tesla stock slips despite Q3 earnings beat, better-than-expected capex spend
articles.summary: Tesla reported Q3 earnings after the bell.
articles.body:
Tesla ( TSLA ) reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings, with its free cash flow and capex spending coming in ahead of Wall Street estimates.

Tesla reported Q3 revenue of $28.05 billion vs. Bloomberg consensus of $28.13 billion. Tesla posted adjusted EPS of $0.48 vs. the $0.44 estimate, with adjusted EBITDA of $3.90 billion vs. $3.66 billion.

Tesla stock fell almost 5% before the bell on Thursday, with Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein claiming the market was reacting to "capacity constraints in the company's auto and battery growth, which could slow near-term growth."

But that might not be the whole story. Tesla reported free cash flow of $1.53 billion vs. an estimated -$4.92 billion, with capital expenditures climbing to $4.732 billion vs. an estimated $7.96 billion for the quarter.

On the earnings call, Tesla updated its full-year capex guidance to $20 billion from $25 billion previously. Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the savings would come from "managing our capital deployment efficiently, and plan to fund [capex] primarily from our cash flows from operations," he said.

"I think capex is actually ending up being a little lower than we anticipated, but we'll start to become more meaningful next year. And then noticeable in the tens of billions in '28," CEO Elon Musk said on the call.

Roundhill CEO Dave Mazza posits the cutting capex means the Tesla isn't transitioning fast enough to an AI-focused company betting on robotaxis, Optimus robots, and compute.

Tesla revealed its Optimus robot started production at its Fremont factory. "While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product," the company said in its earnings release.

"I would expect that it takes us probably at least a year — maybe a little longer — to get to that annualized rate [1 million units], to get to 20,000 units a week," Musk said on the earnings call. Musk added that Tesla may release an Optimus demo video in about a month, stressing that he didn't want the robot's movements to be preplanned.

Regarding its other AI efforts, Tesla said it plans to reach 400 MW of AI training compute by the end of the year. Tesla said its active FSD (full self-driving) subscriptions climbed to 1.74 million.

"The biggest driver of demand is full self-driving," Musk said regarding vehicle sales.

"The Cybercab fleet in Austin has grown by a factor of 10," Musk added while discussing Tesla's robotaxi fleet. He added, "I don't think there's any company in the world that can match our scale with autonomous vehicles."

articles.title: Lockheed lifts annual forecast as missile, jet production ramps up
articles.summary: Oct 22 () - Lockheed Martin raised its full-year sales and profit forecasts on Thursday after posting a rise in ‌third-quarter earnings, helped by strong dem...
articles.body:
Oct 22 (Reuters) - Lockheed Martin ( LMT ) raised its full-year sales and profit forecasts on Thursday after posting a rise in ‌third-quarter earnings, helped by strong demand for its missile ‌defense systems and fighter jets due to ongoing geopolitical conflicts.

The company, a key ​supplier of missile-defense systems such as PAC-3 and THAAD interceptors, joined RTX and Northrop Grumman in raising forecasts this week on strong demand for munitions, air-defense systems and military aircraft.

Lockheed now expects 2026 sales ‌of about $80 billion to $82 ⁠billion, up from its prior forecast of $79.75 billion to $81.75 billion.

The US defense contractor also lifted its annual ⁠earnings-per-share forecast to range between $30.35 and $30.75 from its previous view of $29.95 to $30.65.

The company's backlog rose 27% sequentially to a record $292 billion, boosted ​by a $52.5 ​billion multi-year award for PAC-3 ​Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, stockpiles ‌of which were heavily used by US and allied forces in the Iran war.

Lockheed also raised its 2026 free cash flow forecast to about $7.8 billion to $8 billion, from $7 billion to $7.2 billion earlier.

However, the company warned it remains in negotiations with the US government ‌over production contracts for F-35 Lots ​20 and higher, and said future operations ​and cash flow could ​be affected if additional contractual authorization and funding ‌are not received.

Sales for the quarter ​ended on September ​27 rose 11% to $20.71 billion, driven by 24% growth in its missiles unit on higher PAC-3 and THAAD production and ​a 13% increase ‌in aeronautics revenue from F-35 and C-130 programs.

Profit increased ​14% to $1.85 billion, or $7.97 per share.

(Reporting by Aatreyee Dasgupta ​in Bengaluru; Editing by Leroy Leo)

articles.title: María Cristina Buendía, notaria, sobre la nueva Ley de Propiedad Horizontal: “Si un vecino mayor de 70 años pide un ascensor, la comunidad ya no puede desentenderse”
articles.standfirst: La reforma, que entra en vigor este 23 de octubre, obliga a las comunidades a pedir ayudas para obras de accesibilidad
articles.summary: La reforma, que entra en vigor este 23 de octubre, obliga a las comunidades a pedir ayudas para obras de accesibilidad
articles.body: Las comunidades de propietarios tienen una nueva obligación en el horizonte, y muchas todavía no lo saben. La notaria María Cristina Buendía ha querido advertirlo en un vídeo en redes sociales, en el que explica cómo un cambio legal que entra en vigor esta misma semana puede afectar a la convivencia, y a los gastos, de miles de edificios. “Muy atentas todas las comunidades de propietarios”, avisa. Se refiere a la reforma de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal incluida en la Ley 4/2026, publicada en el BOE el 3 de octubre, que entra en vigor el 23 de octubre de 2026. El cambio afecta a las obras de accesibilidad que pide un vecino con discapacidad o mayor de 70 años. Buendía pone como ejemplo los casos más frecuentes: la instalación de un ascensor o de una rampa. Explica que, si un vecino que cumple esos requisitos solicita estas obras y aporta información sobre las ayudas y subvenciones disponibles en materia de vivienda, “es la comunidad de propietarios la obligada a solicitar estas ayudas”. Y añade: “No puede la junta desentenderse de este trámite”. Hasta ahora, la comunidad no tenía por qué tramitarlas. A partir del 23 de octubre, solicitarlas deja de ser optativo. La segunda novedad tiene que ver con el dinero. Según explica la notaria, si las ayudas realmente concedidas alcanzan el 70% del coste de las obras, ejecutarlas es obligatorio para la comunidad. Hasta ahora ese porcentaje estaba fijado en el 75%. Además, la ley tiene en cuenta las ayudas efectivamente concedidas, no las que la comunidad podría llegar a recibir. Si aun así la comunidad no cumple, Buendía recuerda que ese vecino “puede acudir a un tribunal y ser el juez el que ordene la ejecución” de las obras. Cuando las ayudas concedidas no llegan al 70%, o el coste supera el tope previsto, las obras solo siguen siendo obligatorias si quien las pidió paga la diferencia. La notaria aclara una excepción territorial: la norma no se aplicará en Cataluña, que cuenta con su propia regulación específica en esta materia.

articles.title: Southeast Asia’s toxic haze spurs calls for legal action against polluters
articles.summary: ASEAN’s consensus-driven approach and a lack of enforcement mechanisms make legal action difficult, experts say.
articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – As toxic haze from Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade clouded skies across Malaysia and Singapore over the past two months, a growing clamour of voices has demanded legal accountability.

In theory, a patchwork of domestic and international laws makes it possible for Southeast Asian governments to hold polluters responsible for cross-border haze, most of which has been blamed on land clearing by Indonesian palm oil plantation owners.

In practice, sensitivities around national sovereignty, a lack of enforcement mechanisms, and the practical challenges of evidence collection make legal action difficult, if not infeasible.

On paper, Southeast Asian countries are committed to working together to prevent cross-border air pollution under the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, signed in 2002.

The legally binding treaty commits the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to tackle haze, a recurring issue for decades, through “concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international co-operation”.

However, the agreement does not contain provisions for enforcement by a judicial body such as the International Court of Justice, which requires all parties to consent to its jurisdiction, and disagreements over interpretation and application can only be settled through negotiation.

Implementation of the treaty has also moved at a snail’s pace.

The treaty’s coordinating office, located in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta, only opened this April, nearly a quarter-century after it was envisioned.

“For decades, the response to haze has largely focused on diplomatic engagement, emergency firefighting, and measures to protect public health,” Heng Kiah Chun, a regional campaign strategist for Greenpeace Southeast Asia, told Al Jazeera.

“While these efforts are necessary, they have not sufficiently addressed the underlying causes, including forest and peatland destruction, unsustainable land-use practices and inadequate corporate accountability,” Chun said.

Malaysia and Singapore, where haze has propelled major population centres to the top of global tables for poor air quality, have refrained from criticising Indonesia, instead offering assistance to fight the fires, which are estimated to have burned more than 2 million hectares (about 5 million acres) of land in the archipelago.

Jakarta has given mixed signals on accepting outside assistance, with officials vacillating between welcoming the offers and insisting they can handle the fires themselves.

Mohd Hazmi Mohd Rusli, an associate professor and legal expert at Universiti Sains Islam Malaysia, said Southeast Asia’s long-standing emphasis on consensus and noninterference has hampered action.

“Economic interests and diplomatic considerations also play a role,” Rusli told Al Jazeera.

“Malaysia and Singapore have traditionally favoured diplomatic engagement over direct confrontation in managing sensitive bilateral and regional issues, reflecting ASEAN’s broader preference for consultation and consensus.”

Rather than negotiate new legal frameworks, ASEAN should strengthen its existing treaty “through independent monitoring, clearer compliance procedures, greater corporate accountability and stronger domestic enforcement”, Rusli added.

With diplomatic efforts having little impact, attention has increasingly turned to the possibility of countries using domestic laws with extraterritorial reach, an approach pioneered by Singapore.

Under the 2014 Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, Singaporean authorities are empowered to prosecute polluters for activities taking place overseas, with violators liable for fines of 100,000 Singapore dollars ($78,300) a day up to a maximum of 2 million Singapore dollars ($1.56m).

The act also enables the city-state’s National Environment Agency to issue notices directing companies to cease burning on their lands.

The agency has issued such notices to 10 Indonesia-based firms during this year’s wildfire season. But to date, no company has actually been prosecuted under the Singaporean law.

While the legislation allows authorities to identify suspected polluters through meteorological data, satellite imagery, and maps, prosecutors would likely struggle to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in any case without firsthand evidence from Indonesia.

“Such direct evidence can only be obtained if the Indonesian authorities themselves investigate and take action against these very companies and share their evidence with Singapore,” Alan Khee-Jin Tan, an expert in environmental law at the National University of Singapore (NUS) Faculty of Law, told Al Jazeera.

“The most likely ‘defence’ the companies will take is that the fires started outside their concessions and spread into their holdings.”

Malaysia’s government has said it could consider legislation similar to the Singaporean law, but cautioned that implementation would be difficult.

In 2023, the government abandoned proposals for a law against cross-border haze, citing the difficulty of obtaining evidence for prosecution.

Legal action also risks inflaming diplomatic tensions.

In 2016, Singapore and Indonesia became embroiled in a diplomatic dispute after the city-state’s environmental agency attempted to summon the director of an Indonesian company linked to the haze for questioning.

Indonesia’s then environmental minister, Siti Nurbaya Bakar, accused Singapore of not showing “mutual respect”, a suggestion denied by officials in the city-state.

Tensions have flickered during the latest haze season, too.

On Wednesday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto hit out at countries that “like to insult” his nation over the fires, while pledging to expose foreign companies that he claimed were also responsible for the crisis.

Prabowo said his government took the issue seriously, with authorities arresting individuals found to have started fires, but it would “step up our response”.

The Indonesian leader’s remarks came after a Malaysian politician last week said that Indonesia should be treated as an “outcast” within ASEAN over the haze.

NUS law expert Tan said that while Singaporean authorities could launch a test-case prosecution against Indonesian companies without Jakarta’s assistance, they are unlikely to do so unless Indonesian authorities act first.

“Practically, they are likely to proceed only against those companies which the Indonesian authorities have themselves clearly identified and charged as perpetrators,” he said, adding that a failed prosecution could also expose the legislation as toothless.

“Otherwise, any action that Singapore takes would appear to the Indonesians to be unilateral, and could be politically controversial.”

Eugene Tan Kheng Boon, an associate professor of law at Singapore Management University, said Indonesia’s failure to take stronger action was the ultimate stumbling block to a resolution, but countries could also strengthen their own laws and regulations.

“This could include requiring commodities such as palm oil sold in the region and used in other products to be certified to be sustainably sourced,” Tan told Al Jazeera.

“Customers in the region can also boycott purchasing items from companies that are responsible for the haze,” he said.

“Banks that finance these polluters should also come within the enforcement crosshairs.”

Matthew Baird, director of the Asian Research Institute for Environmental Law, said that stronger political will in the region was needed above all else.

“Governments really have to sit together and work on really good strategic options, like the Chinese government did for air pollution in Beijing, where they were able to reduce air pollution – but it took 30 years and a lot of money,” Baird told Al Jazeera.

“Governments in Southeast Asia have to do it, and they have to get companies to change their behaviour, and that takes time, effort, and probably a lot of litigation,” Baird.

This would involve “holding directors to account, sending directors to jail, holding companies to account, and making sure that they fulfil obligations”, he added.

“Because in every country, it is actually a criminal offence to burn land.”

articles.title: Spotify stock pops on Q3 earnings, driven by premium subscriber growth and AI for personalized experiences
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence helped drive Spotify's third-quarter results
articles.body:
Spotify ( SPOT ) stock rose after reporting Q3 earnings, which showed premium subscribers growing by 9% year-over-year and AI a key part of its strategy moving forward.

The streaming giant posted revenue of nearly €5 billion euros (about $5.6 billion), roughly in line with expectations. Premium subscriptions and ad-supported drove results, up 17% and 10% respectively. Earnings per share came in below expectations at €2.48, less than the €2.80 expected. Gross margin came in at a record 33%, just above the 32.9% Wall Street expected.

"We are very pleased with our performance heading into year-end and view the business as well positioned to deliver improved growth and margins in 2026," the company said in the release.

Shares rose 5% in pre-market trading, a welcomed recovery after falling 6% so far this year.

Monthly active users were up 11% year-over-year to 788 million. For the fourth quarter, it expects to reach 818 million. Revenue is also expected to grow by about 15%.

During the quarter, the company focused on using artificial intelligence to create a more personalized experience, including a taste profile for US Premium users to give insight into their music style. It also launched integration with Meta's Muse.

"By connecting Muse to Spotify, listeners can ask their agent to play music, save songs to their Library, build personalized playlists, find new books, podcasts and more," the release said.

The company also plans to expand audiobooks from 22 markets to 180-plus by the end of the year.

articles.title: Explained: What Double Contributions Convention means for social security benefits of Indians working in UK
articles.summary: Employees movement from one country to another for work usually brings questions around the minimum salary, immigration and taxes.
articles.body: Employees movement from one country to another for work usually brings questions around the minimum salary, immigration and taxes. Such moves can also trigger less obvious social security obligations in both countries, potentially increasing the cost of an international assignment. This was a particular concern for employees moving between India and the UK.Historically, the two countries did not have a bilateral social security agreement as against the other European countries with whom India has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) i.e. Belgium, Germany, France, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, Luxembourg, Portugal and Sweden.Therefore, an employee temporarily sent from India to the UK could, subject to conditions, remain outside the UK National Insurance Contributions (UK NICs) for up to 52 weeks as per the UK social security laws. However, once this period ended, UK contributions could become relevant even where contributions continued in India.The position could be even more immediate for employees moving from the UK to India, who could fall within India's social security regime as International Workers (IWs) from the start of their assignment. In practical terms, an international assignment could therefore result in social security contributions becoming payable in both countries.Against this backdrop, social security became an important part of the broader India-UK economic trade discussions. The two governments ultimately concluded a Double Contributions Convention (DCC) to provide a framework for determining social security contribution obligations for eligible employees moving between the two countries. The DCC, which came into force on 15 July 2026, is intended to address the risk of double social security contributions on qualifying international assignments. Here are the key features of this Agreement alongside practical issues which require clarifications.Key features of the AgreementThe basic rule: pay social security in one countryThe agreement is designed so that an employee is generally subject to one country's legislation (UK/India). A qualifying employee may continue under the home country's social-security system where he/she:is an employed person in the home country;works for an employer which normally carries out its activities there;is sent by that employer to the other country to work on its behalf; andis expected to work in the host country for no more than 60 months.Put simply, an employee sent from India to work temporarily in the UK for up to five years can, if the conditions are fulfilled, remain subject to Indian social security instead of paying UK NICs. Conversely, a qualifying employee sent from the UK to India can remain subject to UK social-security legislation and continue paying UK NICs rather than Indian social-security contribution. This is a major practical simplification for international mobile employees and their employers.India-to-UK assignments: Social security position before and after the DCCUK-to-India assignments: Social security position before and after the DCCBefore you leave: existing social security contributions mattersAs per the UK tax and social security authorities (HMRC), to get the benefit of detachment (i.e. relief from double contribution) under the Agreement, the employee must already have been covered by the social security system of his home country before the assignment starts. The employee and employer must have paid, or be treated as having paid, contributions for at least 30 days before the employee leaves the home country, or for the calendar month before the temporary assignment begins.This makes pre-departure planning particularly important. HR and global mobility teams should check the employee's social security status before the assignment starts rather than trying to resolve the position after the employee has already moved.Certificate of coverage: an important piece of paperworkThe Certificate of Coverage (COC) becomes an important document under the new framework. In practical terms, it provides evidence that an employee remains covered by the social security system of the home country while temporarily working in the other country. An employee who remains covered under India's social security system while working in the UK should obtain a COC from the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO). This provides evidence that Indian social security contributions continue to apply and that UK NICs are not due under the DCC. Similarly, an employee remaining within UK social security while working in India, may apply to HMRC for a UK COC using Form CA9107.Employers should therefore make the COC process part of their standard pre-departure checklist, alongside immigration, payroll and tax requirements. The EPFO has also updated its online portal to facilitate COC applications for eligible employees under the India-UK DCC.Five years of social security protection does not mean five years of visa-free workThis distinction deserves emphasis. The DCC determines where social-security contributions are paid. It does not itself confer a right to enter, stay or work in the other country. The UK Government's DCC explainer specifically says that nothing in the arrangement changes the UK's immigration regime or its ability to control its borders.An employee still needs to satisfy the applicable immigration requirements to work in the UK. Therefore, social-security coverage and immigration permission are two separate compliance requirements.An employee could potentially satisfy the DCC conditions for social-security purposes but still needs an appropriate Visa and sponsorship arrangements to perform the proposed work in the host country.What if an assignment is extended An assignment that is extended after it begins does not automatically lose protection under the DCC. For example, if an employee is sent from London to Mumbai for three years and the project is later extended to five and a half years, the employee may remain covered by the UK social security system until the assignment ends or the 60-month limit is reached, whichever is earlier.HMRC illustrates this with a UK employee who’s planned 24-month assignment is extended to 66 months and clarifies that UK legislation continues to apply for the first 60 months, after which Indian social security legislation applies.Waiting period between two consecutive assignmentsThe DCC includes an anti-reset rule to prevent employers or employees from repeatedly starting fresh assignments to extend home-country social security coverage within the overall period of 60 months. Generally, once a detached-worker assignment ends, the employee must wait six months before a new qualifying assignment can begin. If the earlier assignment lasted less than six months, the required waiting period is equal to the length of that assignment.Remote working cases may also includeReflecting the growth of cross-border remote working, the Agreement may also cover employees who temporarily choose to work from the other country for personal reasons, provided their employer agrees and the other prescribed conditions are met. HMRC’s guidance illustrates this with employees who temporarily work overseas to join a partner or to be closer to elderly family members.In such cases, the employee may qualify as a ‘detached worker’ (i.e. eligible for benefit under the Agreement) and remain covered by the social security system of the home country. This flexibility is particularly relevant for multinational employers developing cross-border remote-working policies.Watch out for assignments that started before 15 July 2026Special transitional rules apply to employees who were already on assignment when the DCC came into force on 15 July 2026. HMRC’s guidance clarifies that such employees do not automatically qualify as ‘detached workers’ (i.e. eligible for benefit under the Agreement). For example, an employee of an Indian employer who was working in the UK immediately before that date (15 July 2026) under the existing 52-week period, NIC exemption became subject to UK social security legislation from 15 July 2026, rather than receiving a new 60-month exemption under the DCC. A corresponding principle applies to relevant UK employees who were already working in India. This distinction between assignments already underway and those beginning on or after 15 July 2026 is therefore particularly important for employers’ global mobility and payroll teams.Employees who regularly work in both countriesThe position is more complex for employees who normally divide their work between India and the UK, as the DCC does not provide a special rule for this working pattern. However, HMRC clarifies that in such cases, UK NICs shall be payable on earnings from work performed in the UK and Indian social security contribution being payable on earnings from work performed in India. This differs significantly from a straightforward temporary assignment covered by the 60-month detached-worker rule. As international hybrid-working arrangements become more common, employers will therefore need to review each arrangement carefully rather than assume that the five-year rule removes every cross-border social security obligation.What the DCC does not doThe benefits of the DCC should also be considered alongside its limitations. First, it is fundamentally a contributions coordination agreement, not a comprehensive social security benefits agreement. The UK Government expressly explains that the DCC does not govern access to benefits such as the UK State Pension or change the rules determining access to benefits. Second, this Agreement does not apply to self-employment cases. Third, the Agreement itself does not change immigration rules. Employers should therefore treat social security, personal taxation, payroll, immigration and employment law as independent compliance matters. An exemption under one regime does not automatically settle the others.Areas where further guidance would be helpfulThe DCC and HMRC’s guidance explain the core contribution rules, but additional practical guidance from HMRC, the EPFO and other relevant Indian authorities would help employers apply them consistently. Official FAQs with illustrations would be useful, especially on the following issues.Hybrid and recurring cross-border working - HMRC clearly recognises employer-approved personal-choice remote working to qualify as detached worker. Some practical instances would be particularly useful for employees whose arrangements sit between traditional detachment and regular two-country working. For example, how should an employer analyse an employee who ordinarily works in India but is permitted to work from the UK for several weeks every quarter? How should the position differ where that pattern is agreed in advance for several years?Indian payroll and the contribution base – There is lack of clarity on the “wage” on which Indian social security contributions should be calculated while an Indian employee is detached to the UK. For Indian employees temporarily assigned to the UK, it is provided that employee and employer contributions in India are to be calculated on the total wages, determined under the Indian social security legislation. This raises an important practical question for payroll teams, particularly where contributions before the assignment were based on the statutory wage ceiling (i.e. at INR 25,000 per month) or on employee’s basic salary and not on total wages. A clear guidance on the applicable contribution base that should apply while a COC is in force and whether, on the employee’s return to India, such base may revert to the basis that applied before the UK assignment. Specific examples covering different categories of employees and establishments would help employers apply the provision consistently and plan their costs.Changes in employment during the assignment – What happens when the factual assumptions supporting the original COC change. Common examples include:transfer of employment to another group company;change of employing entity following a corporate restructuring;split or shadow payroll arrangements;a substantial extension in the expected duration of the assignment;transition from temporary assignment to local employment; ormovement from a conventional expatriate arrangement to a recurring hybrid-working pattern.These situations should not automatically be treated as continuing to qualify merely because the original COC covered a period of up to 60 months. In practice, employers may need to reassess whether the conditions supporting the original coverage continue to be satisfied. A clarification from authorities will help accordingly.Ongoing assignments as on 15 July 2026 – The agreement provides that the ongoing assignments as on 15 July 2026 shall not be covered. But that leaves practical questions for employers seeking to reorganise legitimate assignments.For example, can an existing assignment formally end and a genuinely new assignment subsequently begin? If so, what conditions must be satisfied before that new assignment can qualify for benefit under the Agreement? How should short-term assignments (upto 1 year period) that were still within the 52-week domestic-law exemption be handled? These are precisely the situations in which coordinated FAQs and worked examples from HMRC, EPFO and the relevant authorities would give employers much-needed certainty.Welcome step forward, but careful implementation is keyThe DCC is a significant step forward for employee mobility between India and the UK, as it provides a clear framework for determining where social security contributions are payable during a qualifying temporary assignment. Its benefit should not, however, be described as a blanket five-year exemption: eligible detached workers remain covered by one country’s social security system, subject to the conditions of the Agreement, rather than being exempt from contributions altogether.Employers should therefore assess eligibility before departure, obtain and maintain the appropriate COC, and review the position whenever assignment terms or working arrangements change. With sound planning and further administrative guidance, the DCC should reduce double-contribution costs, improve compliance certainty and make cross-border talent deployment between the two countries more efficient.(The author, Ravi Jain is Tax Partner at Vialto. Vikas Kumar, Director, and Pawan Digga, Manager at Vialto, have also contributed to this article. Views are personal. Note: This article is intended as a general explanation of the new arrangements and not as tax, immigration, employment-law or social-security advice for a particular employee or assignment.)You use AI every day. articles.title: Airbnb cambia las normas del alquiler de pisos turísticos: prohibe que los huéspedes laven los platos, saquen la basura o limpien
articles.standfirst: La plataforma limita las peticiones abusivas de salida que solían realizar los anfitriones
articles.summary: La plataforma limita las peticiones abusivas de salida que solían realizar los anfitriones
articles.body: Airbnb cambia las normas del alquiler de los pisos turísticos. Uno de los inconvenientes más criticados por los usuarios llegaba al finalizar su estancia: la extensa lista de tareas de salida. Entre ellas solían estar desde dejar las sábanas quitadas o sacar la basura solían ser exigencias habituales, pero la plataforma de alquileres de corta duración ha actualizado sus normas para limitar estas peticiones por parte de los anfitriones. A través de su nueva política comunitaria, Airbnb establece que "no se podrá exigir a los huéspedes tareas que requieran un esfuerzo o tiempo significativos, o que habitualmente correspondan al personal de limpieza". Por ejemplo, ya no podrán solicitarte que friegues y guardes la vajilla, aunque sí será razonable pedirte que la dejes recogida en el fregadero. Desde la compañía señalan que la actualización responde a las quejas de la comunidad sobre reglas confusas y engorrosas. Con este rediseño buscan garantizar que las solicitudes se mantengan en un nivel razonable, garantizando transparencia y evitando sorpresas desagradables al abandonar el inmueble. Como parte de este cambio, las reglas de la casa serán más visibles y se mostrarán en la página del anuncio, en la pestaña de viajes y en los recordatorios de la reserva. Habrá siete normas estándar sobre horarios, número de huéspedes, tabaco, mascotas, horas de silencio y uso comercial del espacio. Aunque los anfitriones podrán añadir peticiones adicionales siempre que sean razonables, Airbnb supervisará las publicaciones. Cualquier solicitud que incumpla la normativa será marcada para su eliminación o revisión, garantizando así un estándar uniforme para todos los usuarios. Finalmente, la plataforma recuerda que la tarifa de limpieza abonada solo debe cubrir la puesta a punto estándar del alojamiento. Por ello, queda totalmente prohibido que los anfitriones cobren recargos o penalizaciones a los clientes por no realizar tareas de salida no autorizadas.

articles.title: US to award $389 million in R&D funds for power semiconductors, critical materials
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The US Commerce Department said on Thursday it plans to award $389 million in research and development funding to four compani...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The US Commerce Department said on Thursday it plans to award $389 million in ‌research and development funding to four companies working ‌on power semiconductor devices and critical materials, with the government receiving ​minority equity stakes.

The department in recent months has awarded 19 R&D grants to semiconductor firms from a $10 billion fund approved by Congress in 2022. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ‌said in a ⁠statement the awards will "accelerate American semiconductor innovation to enhance our domestic energy and power resources."

The ⁠department said it had signed letters of intent to provide four new awards:

• Helion will receive up to $175 ​million to ​develop high-voltage power semiconductors ​and advanced energy power ‌modules

in fusion power generation. The semiconductors will power and use energy from magnets driving Helion fusion generators.

• Commonwealth Fusion Systems will receive up to $85 million to develop semiconductors for radio-frequency plasma heating, power electronics, fusion diagnostics, and ‌radiation-hardened electronics.

• Vertical Semiconductor will ​receive up to $73 million to ​advance its vertical gallium ​nitride power semiconductors for use in AI ‌data center racks.

• Sibelco will ​receive up ​to $56 million to develop next-generation purification for ultra-high-purity quartz used in the semiconductor supply chain.

The department said ​as a condition ‌of funding, the US government will receive minority, ​non-controlling and non-voting equity stakes.

(Reporting by David ​Shepardson; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

articles.title: Thousands of cans of Walmart-brand fruit cocktail recalled
articles.summary: More than 40,000 cans of fruit cocktail are impacted.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Possible lead contamination has prompted the recall of thousands of cans of Walmart’s Great Value-branded fruit cocktail.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday designated the recall as Class II , meaning that consumption or exposure to the recalled fruit cocktail could “cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.”

According to the recall notice , more than 44,000 cans of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate may have been contaminated with elevated levels of lead.

The 15-ounce cans have a lot code of 6FCB 04 C2263 and a “best if used by” date of “SEP 01 2027” printed on them.

They were distributed to Walmart stores in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wyoming. The recall was initiated on Oct. 1, meaning the impacted cans are likely no longer on store shelves.

No other lots or Great Value products are impacted in the recall.

If you do have a can of fruit cocktail that matches the above lot and date codes, you are advised not to eat it. There’s no safe level of lead, according to the FDA .

Earlier this month, multiple varieties of frozen berries sold at Walmart and Trader Joe’s stores in 33 states were recalled over possible E. coli contamination.

articles.title: Marshall blames Ukraine war for high diesel prices
articles.summary: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) on Wednesday blamed the war in Ukraine for high diesel prices, with energy costs as a key concern in the rapidly approaching midterms. “The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is No. 1, is the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down. But beyond…
articles.body:
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) on Wednesday blamed the war in Ukraine for high diesel prices, with energy costs as a key concern in the rapidly approaching midterms.

“The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is No. 1, is the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down. But beyond that, why are we dependent upon diesel imports?” Marshall said during a Senate debate against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

“It’s because of the Green New Deal policy that my opponent supports. His policies would fit in just right with Chuck Schumer. So, if I would lose this seat, Adam Hamilton would give control of the Senate to Chuck Schumer, who would go back to his Green New Deal,” the Kansas senator added, referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

Multiple factors are behind the recent rise in diesel prices, including the ongoing war in Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war. In the case of the war in Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed amid the conflict. When it comes to the Russia-Ukraine war, Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries are also pushing diesel prices higher.

Energy costs have become a key issue in the 2026 midterms as the GOP fights to maintain control of Congress. According to AAA, the average cost of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. on Thursday morning was about $6.31, up from about $3.63 last year at the same time .

The race between Hamilton and Marshall is rated as a “toss-up” by the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report, which is notable given that Kansas has not elected a Democrat for Senate since the 1930s.

Other issues weighing the GOP down in this year’s midterms include President Trump’s unpopularity and concerns about the cost of living.

When reached for comment, the Hamilton campaign noted comments during the debate in which the Kansas Democrat said he did not “support the Green New Deal,” but rather “parts of it.”

“Adam supports all of the above energy production and believes Kansans should decide what happens on their land,” the campaign said in a statement.

The Hill has also reached out to Schumer’s office for comment.

articles.title: KFC switches to Coke. But Pepsi’s still king at Taco Bell
articles.summary: KFC dumped PepsiCo last week, but its sister chain Taco Bell announced Thursday it’s keeping the Mountain Dew Baja Blast maker on for another decade.
articles.body: KFC dumped PepsiCo last week, but its sister chain Taco Bell announced Thursday it’s keeping the Mountain Dew Baja Blast maker on for another decade. The Taco Bell deal is a much-needed win for PepsiCo, whose business has had rough few weeks. Not only did it lose its longstanding contract with KFC to rival Coca-Cola, but its drink business in North America is also in a slump. The company reported a 2% decline for its North America beverage unit during its most recent quarter, and its CEO Ramon Laguarta bluntly said on its earnings call that it’s “not competing well in soft drinks,” including newly acquired Poppi brand. Losing the KFC contract is a blow for PepsiCo, considering it once owned the fried chicken chain. But keeping Taco Bell is a bigger deal, since the latter has generated $17 billion in US system-wide sales last year compared to KFC’s roughly $5 billion. (Both chains are owned by Yum! Brands.) Taco Bell and PepsiCo said in a statement that the two will continue collaborating on new beverages and foods until 2036, including upcoming new flavors for their Doritos Locos Tacos. It also noted that the Baja Blast drink has become a $1 billion brand. As food prices rise and consumers look to cut back, the beverage category is a key growth area for Taco Bell and other fast food chains. Taco Bell is aggressively expanding its beverage sales aiming to generate $5 billion in revenue by 2030. Last year, the chain released a lineup of “Refrescas” drinks aimed at attracting consumers searching for a beverage between meals. Further expansion will come from developing new Baja Blast options with Pepsi, including a limited-time pink lemonade with singer Olivia Rodrigo. “Taco Bell’s Baja Blast lineup has often been a key differentiator for the brand, and leaning into product exclusives can help drive visitation to quick service restaurant chains,” Elizabeth Lafontaine, director of research at location analytics firm Placer.ai, previously told CNN. “Especially as the industry faces steeper competition and consumers who are on the hunt for more value from fast food offerings,” she added. Taco Bell and PepsiCo said in a statement that they plan to stay ahead on “emerging beverage trends across crafted, functional and energy beverages, including energy offerings designed to appeal to Gen Z consumers and unlock new morning and afternoon occasions.” Taco Bell has been a bright spot in the fast food industry, but saw a traffic decline over the summer due toa cyclospora outbreak that was linked to lettuce served at a number of restaurants. The company will give a fuller view of the sales impact when it releases earnings next month.

articles.title: Civil servant who juggled five jobs 'wasn't thinking straight'
articles.summary: Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs.
articles.body:
A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs has told the court he "wasn't thinking straight" when he allegedly misled future bosses about his employment status.

Kashim Chowdhury said he was "in a panic" when he applied for a job at the Department of Health (DHSC), failing to declare he was already working at the Department for the Environment (Defra).

The prosecution said he already had three full-time jobs at the time, including roles at the London Borough of Tower Hamlets and East London NHS Trust.

The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

Chowdhury said he was "in a panic'' because he feared losing his Defra job and was uncertain about his future. He told the jury he was "not paying attention, I was not thinking straight',' when filling out the application.

The prosecution said Chowdhury held five jobs on full-time salaries at the height of the alleged deceit.

Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears

Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs

In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office.

The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work-from-home culture which began during the Covid-19 pandemic to hide his multiple jobs and took sick leave from some employers to manage the workload.

But Chowdhury told the court he had not wanted the jobs at the DHSC, Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office.

He told the jury: ''I sent out a flurry of these applications. The offers for these jobs came all at once. I had discussions with my line managers saying that I did not want these jobs and explained my circumstances. These were all short term and probationary and my priority was to look after my mother.''

He added that around May and June 2022, his mother's health "deteriorated".

He said: "That overwhelmed me at the time. It just destroyed me."

Chowdhury described the jobs as his "lifeline at the time".

"They gave me a link to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time."

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity".

articles.title: Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: Rising costs leave US workers juggling multiple jobs as financial security becomes increasingly elusive.
articles.body:
Stacy Eichel, an empty nester in Florida, spent years balancing two jobs. One was in healthcare; the other was her own venture: a small business making custom-branded merchandise for corporate clients, such as coffee mugs and T-shirts that companies hand out at conferences and holiday parties.

For Eichel, the business was more than a paycheque. It was a side hustle for a woman who couldn’t sit still, who was always hungry for the next opportunity. It was the kind of business that thrived when companies had a little extra to spend on small branded trinkets to make an otherwise mundane corporate conference something memorable.

In September 2025, Eichel lost her job in marketing for a healthcare company after a merger. Suddenly, the business she had run on the side had to shoulder more of the burden of supporting her. Yet just as she needed it to provide more, the market for her products was shrinking.

Faced with uncertainty over trade policy and tariffs, alongside the growing use of artificial intelligence across the economy, companies have been tightening their spending. Custom-branded merchandise was becoming one more expense they could do without.

“The economy is such that fewer people are buying custom-branded swag because it’s more of a luxury item. When they have extra money in the budget, that’s what they’ll use it for, but now their budgets are very tight,” Eichel, who has cut back on her expenses, told Al Jazeera.

Eichel’s experience reflects a broader strain in the US labour market, where a paycheque does not necessarily translate into financial security. The headline unemployment rate captures people actively looking for work, but it does not tell the whole story of people who are working fewer hours than they want or juggling jobs that do not provide enough income.

The Department of Labor documents this through what is called the U-6 rate, a broader measure of unemployment and underemployment. It stands at an elevated 7.6 percent. While that’s down from 8.1 percent a year ago, having a job does not necessarily mean Americans are getting ahead financially.

The U-6 measure includes people who are working part-time because they cannot find full-time jobs, as well as those who want to work but have stopped looking for a job recently.

Even people who are employed full-time are finding that their earnings do not stretch as far as they once did. An estimated 4.5 million Americans were working part-time because they could not find full-time work. Meanwhile, nine million Americans held multiple jobs, accounting for 5.5 percent of all employed workers, according to the most recent jobs report.

“Underemployment is one of the most misunderstood economic problems in America because it doesn’t always look like unemployment. It looks like a college graduate working retail despite having a degree, a former executive accepting a position paying half their previous salary, or a parent working two jobs because neither provides enough hours, benefits or income to support their family,” Tara Furiani, a workforce strategist based in Richmond, Virginia, told Al Jazeera.

Average hourly wages rose 3 percent over the past year, while consumer prices increased 3.7 percent, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the US Labor Department.

That means prices have risen faster than wages, leaving many workers with less purchasing power. Overall, prices rose 0.6 percent from the previous month, while average hourly wages increased by just 0.1 percent, adding to the financial pressure on households like Eichel’s.

Eichel has cut back on expenses and scaled down some of her usual spending, including dining out and takeout, and dropped her cable service.

“I never used to think before ordering in, and now we cook everything,” Eichel said.

With the midterm elections approaching, the cost of living is becoming a greater concern for voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that the cost of living was the most important issue for voters, leading the next-closest issue by a double-digit margin, at 47 percent compared with 22 percent for “democratic norms and values”.

A separate Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy, 40 percent to 33 percent, marking the first time in 12 years that Democrats have held an advantage on the issue.

This comes as 44 percent of Americans said they had struggled to pay for at least one basic necessity over the past year, including transportation, rent or mortgage payments, medical care and food, according to a Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month.

Twenty percent of respondents said they had received food from a food bank or pantry over the past year.

Joshua Teicher, a New York City-based video producer in the advertising industry, said work began drying up after the COVID-19 pandemic, with opportunities dwindling further in recent years as companies tightened their budgets. Even the slow trickle of work has nearly dried up entirely.

Teicher told Al Jazeera that his financial circumstances have changed so significantly that he is now on Medicaid, government-subsidised healthcare for people in lower-income brackets. He said he is struggling to afford prescriptions and food.

“I’m having to go into my savings. Specifically, sometimes I don’t want to get a second cup of coffee because it’s like five bucks for an espresso or something like that. It’s also been harder to eat healthy. Grocery shopping, apples are just ridiculous. I find myself walking a couple of extra blocks to a cheaper store because they have cheaper apples, those sorts of things,” Teicher said.

He told Al Jazeera that his tight budget also prevents him from affording the knee surgery he needs. Cartilage in both knees has worn down. He was able to undergo surgery on his right knee to correct the problem, but cannot afford the same procedure on his left. As a result, one leg is now slightly longer than the other.

Petrol prices are another expense weighing on consumers. The average price for a gallon of gasoline (3.78 litres) on Monday was $4.29, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks fuel prices daily. By comparison, the average price was $2.98 when the US and Israel first struck Iran in late February, leading to ongoing disruptions in the global market.

Even for Americans who have jobs, finding a better-paying position can be difficult. Although some industries have continued to add jobs, uncertainty about economic policy has contributed to what economists call a “low-hire, low-fire” labour market.

Employers are pulling back on hiring even as layoffs remain relatively low. The latest Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that job openings and the number of workers quitting their jobs were largely unchanged.

“I have seen highly qualified people who have not been able to find a job for 12-18 months,” Babak Hafezi, a professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera.

With fewer opportunities available, workers who already have jobs may be reluctant to leave them, even if they are unhappy or want higher pay. Those looking for work face more competition for available positions, while people who are already employed may have less leverage to negotiate better salaries. That can make it harder for workers to improve their financial situations as everyday expenses continue to rise. This is leading some people who already work full-time to add on part-time jobs.

“We have people come in all the time who are teachers looking for a part-time job, or who are in other fields asking, ‘Do you know anyone hiring part-time? I just need 15–20 hours a week to make ends meet.’ At what point does this end?” Debbie Louis, who owns a coffee shop in Brooklyn, New York, told Al Jazeera.

Although industries such as hospitality and healthcare have added jobs over the last year, Hafezi said that growth could slow or reverse over the next year. He pointed to the potential impact of the Big Beautiful tax legislation, which could reduce funding for programmes that support rural hospitals , as well as immigration policies that have discouraged international travel to the US over the past year, hitting businesses that benefit from those revenues.

At the same time, US consumers are also dealing with the reality of reduced purchasing power.

“Tariffs and economic pressures from high inflation are affecting Americans’ purchasing power. As prices increase, unit consumption decreases [they buy less as] their paycheques don’t go as far,” Hafezi said.

“This ultimately leads Americans to feel poorer and less able to consume. That is the environment that many Americans in the ‘K-shaped’ economy are in.”

In a so-called K-shaped economy, wealthier US consumers continue to prosper while lower- and middle-income households fall behind. The Conference Board’s most recent consumer confidence report found that higher-income households, often supported by investment gains and greater financial reserves, are more optimistic than those in other income brackets.

“Ahead of the midterms, policymakers and employers should be examining not simply how many Americans are working, but whether available employment provides adequate wages, sufficient hours, predictable schedules, benefits and genuine opportunities for advancement. Because a paycheque and economic security are, again, not the same thing,” Furiani, the workforce strategist, added.

articles.title: Market sell-off gains steam as concerns about Iran war and high AI spending collide
articles.summary: U.S. equity markets sold off sharply as fears that Israel and the U.S. would attack Iran sent oil prices higher, while stocks failed to hold onto recent gains.
articles.body: U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the United States would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold onto recent gains. The S&P 500 was down 1.4% by midmorning, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq saw declines of 2.2%. The price of international Brent crude climbed more than 2%, while U.S. crude gained more than 1%. Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the last several months — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets as riskier ones like tech stocks sold off. That sent bond yields lower. The broad sell-off was sparked in part by reporting Wednesday that Israel and the U.S. were preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections. Likely targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to The New York Times. U.S. military and diplomatic personnel were also being evacuated from several countries in the Middle East on Wednesday, NBC News reported. Iranian officials have promised widespread retaliation to any strikes, pointing to critical Middle East data center sites and undersea internet cables as potential targets. Major tech stocks led the declines in early trading, with Meta and Tesla sliding after both companies reported quarterly earnings Wednesday evening. Meta’s earnings and revenues beat forecasts, but only after excluding billions of dollars in legal penalties the company paid last quarter. It also warned investors that it expects to increase its spending in the coming year to meet demands for computing power. A separate regulatory filing revealed that Meta intends to spend an additional $825 billion on contracts related to its AI infrastructure buildout. Tesla, meanwhile, said it was reining in its capital spending plans, disappointing investors who were hoping for a signal of more aggressive expansion. The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday morning after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments. U.S. markets remain near all-time highs. But signs of flagging returns on the AI investment boom have resulted in more intense gyrations lately. A major sell-off in French government debt has also dragged European stocks lower in recent weeks. “It’s been another difficult 24 hours for markets, as investors grapple with AI growth concerns, higher oil prices, and ongoing fiscal stress,” wrote Henry Allen, director and macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, in a note to clients Thursday. A significant market drawdown may also put a further dent in Republicans’ midterm elections outlook. President Donald Trump frequently points to solid stock market gains as evidence that his economic agenda has made Americans richer. A significant market stumble ahead of the Nov. 3 election would undermine a core argument for Trump and the GOP.

articles.title: Meta stock drops more than 6% despite strong Q3 results, stock split
articles.summary: Meta stock fell more than 6% Thursday.
articles.body:
Meta ( META ) stock plunged more than 6% on Thursday, despite reporting better-than-anticipated Q3 revenue results after the bell on Wednesday.

The declines come as i nvestors continue to pull back on semiconductor and other AI stocks amid ongoing concerns about data center spending and returns on massive AI investments.

Meta raised the lower end of its capital expenditure estimates to between $135 billion and $145 billion from $130 billion and $145 billion. The company also has $825 billion in various spending commitments related to cloud capacity arrangements, energy service agreements, and consumer hardware products.

Despite Wall Street's reaction to Meta's earnings, analysts were largely bullish on the company's outlook, owing to its prospects for its Muse AI agent and models.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg repeatedly pointed to Muse as a source of growth potential during the company's earnings call, saying "Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years," as long as compute efficiency in AI systems continues to improve.

Meta posted an all-time high revenue of $64 billion in the quarter, well ahead of the $63.3 billion analysts anticipated. GAAP earnings per share came in at $3.83 versus expectations of $3.56, but would have been $7.40 without legal charges related to the company's teen mental health settlement.

The company also announced it will issue new non-voting Class C shares to all Class A stockholders , effectively creating a 2-for-1 stock split. The move is meant to ensure Zuckerberg stays in California and retains voting control of the company if the state's Proposition 40 passes on Election Day.

Prop. 40 calls for a 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion.

Ahead of Meta's earnings report, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion in connection with the state's consumer-harms case against the social media giant.

articles.title: Chip stocks break a bear trap after a $3 trillion rout — here are the levels bulls need to hold
articles.summary: A $2.7 trillion chip sell-off is putting the floor under Tuesday's bear trap to its third test.
articles.body:
Chip bulls sprang a bear trap on Tuesday. Two sessions later, the floor under it has cracked.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is down about 6% Thursday, slicing below 11,000 — the support that rescued the group twice since September. A bear trap is a breakdown that quickly reverses, catching traders who bet on further losses. This one only worked as long as that floor held.

The index is on track for its worst day since July and its lowest close since July 29.

All 60 stocks in a Yahoo Finance chip basket are down since Oct. 6, erasing about $3 trillion in market value, more than $800 billion of it Thursday alone. Lam Research ( LRCX ) and Applied Materials ( AMAT ) have each lost nearly 30% in that span, and AMD ( AMD ) more than 20%. Nvidia ( NVDA ) has fallen less, but on its size that's more than $600 billion.

Lam is leading Thursday's slide after reporting record revenue Wednesday night. The company said supply limits capped its outlook and that China sales will be "meaningfully down" in December.

The selling isn't sparing the giants. Meta ( META ) is shedding about $100 billion in market value after its earnings, and SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) are sliding too. Still, the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) is down about 7% since Oct. 6. Chips are down nearly three times as much.

The index closed near 11,130 on Sept. 14 and again on Oct. 16. Tuesday's dip into that zone reversed sharply, springing the trap.

Thursday's break puts the 10,450-10,550 zone in focus. That's where the summer rally started on July 29. The 200-day moving average sits just above it.

On the upside, bulls first need to win back 11,000, then 12,600-12,700. That area capped rallies in August and September.

Semiconductor ETFs saw record flows over the past week, Bloomberg senior ETF analyst Eric Balchunas posted Thursday. "Buying the dip here has [a] pretty good record of working," he wrote.

There's little room to hide from the AI trade. "Every index on the planet is basically an AI index," Matt Miskin, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife John Hancock Investments, said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

Watch whether buyers can pull the index back above 11,000 by the close. A close above it keeps the bulls' hopes alive, while a close below puts the 10,500 area in play.
